body.statement:
For every population tuple covered by \(	ext{thm:complete-effect-image}\) and every \(u,v\in V\), singletonness follows by direct equality comparison in the displayed image. Precisely, \( |S_{vu}(W,\mathcal G(W,\ell),\ell)|=1\) if and only if one of the following mutually compatible branches holds: \(v=u\); \(v
e u\) and \(g_{\mathcal G,\ell}(u)= ot\); or \(v
e u\), \(g_{\mathcal G,\ell}(u)\in[k]\), and either \(L_u(W,\mathcal G,\ell)=\varnothing\), or \(z_u(W,\mathcal G,\ell)=1\) with \(W_{vc}=0\) for every \(c\in L_u(W,\mathcal G,\ell)\), or \(z_u(W,\mathcal G,\ell)=0\), \(L_u(W,\mathcal G,\ell)
e\varnothing\), and \(W_{vc}W_{ud}-W_{vd}W_{uc}=0\) for every \(c,d\in L_u(W,\mathcal G,\ell)\). The common value is one when \(v=u\), zero on the fixed singleton-mleaf branch and on either cogent-group branch admitting zero, and \(W_{vc}/W_{uc}\) for any admissible \(c\in L_u(W,\mathcal G,\ell)\) in the remaining branch.
body.justification: This transparent algebraic corollary tells a consumer how to read singletonness and its common value directly from the exact image.
body.gap: The contribution is the complete mixed-DOG image; the zero and cross-multiplication conditions are its direct finite-set equality test and are not advertised as an independently defined certification theorem.
body.consumer: An analyst can test whether the reported finite image collapses without introducing a second diagnostic object whose definition merely restates singletonness.
body.proof_tex:
The complete-image theorem reduces the question to equality of the finitely many values in the displayed definition of \(S_{vu}\). If \(v=u\), then \(S_{uu}=\{1\}\). If \(v\ne u\) and \(g_{\mathcal G,\ell}(u)=\bot\), then \(S_{vu}=\{0\}\). These prove the first two branches and their common values.

Suppose \(v\ne u\) and \(g_{\mathcal G,\ell}(u)=g\in[k]\). Every \(c\in L_u\) occurs as a legal pivot paired with center \(u\), so
\[
W_{uc}\ne0\qquad(c\in L_u).
\]
If \(L_u=\varnothing\), nonemptiness of the finite argmin \(\Omega^\star\) implies that some projected pair in \(P_g\) has center different from \(u\). Hence \(z_u=1\) and \(S_{vu}=\{0\}\).

If \(z_u=1\), zero belongs to \(S_{vu}\). The set is a singleton if and only if every ratio also equals zero. By the nonzero-denominator condition,
\[
\frac{W_{vc}}{W_{uc}}=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
W_{vc}=0,
\]
so this is equivalent to \(W_{vc}=0\) for every \(c\in L_u\), and the common value is zero. This argument includes the empty \(L_u\) case vacuously.

It remains to consider \(z_u=0\) and nonempty \(L_u\). There is no adjoined zero, so singletonness is equivalent to equality of all ratios. For any \(c,d\in L_u\), both denominators are nonzero and
\[
\frac{W_{vc}}{W_{uc}}=\frac{W_{vd}}{W_{ud}}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
W_{vc}W_{ud}-W_{vd}W_{uc}=0.
\]
Thus all ratios are equal if and only if every displayed \(2\times2\) minor vanishes. When they do, the common value is \(W_{vc}/W_{uc}\) for any \(c\in L_u\). The case analysis is exhaustive and proves both directions of every branch in the proposition.
